analysis.one_liner: Blocks ICE from creating new warehouse, tent, or modular immigration detention facilities.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2026 by Rep. Rashida Tlaib with 25 Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in a House subcommittee with no committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit the Department of Homeland Security and ICE from entering into or renewing any contract or agreement to create a new immigration detention model — warehouses, industrial buildings, tents, soft-sided structures, modular units, and processing centers. It would bar existing federal funds from being spent or reprogrammed for those facilities and direct money already obligated for them to affordable health care and housing instead. The bill's findings describe ICE's announced plan to spend roughly $38.3 billion converting warehouses into large-scale detention centers, and cite 33 reported deaths in immigration detention in 2025 and 13 so far in 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants who could be detained in the new facilities, their families and communities, and taxpayers, who would not fund a multi-billion-dollar expansion of detention sites in converted warehouses and tents. Communities near the facilities would avoid the water, power, and infrastructure strain the bill describes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Detained immigrants, their families, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would stop ICE from establishing, operating, expanding, converting, or renovating any warehouse, industrial facility, tent, soft-sided structure, or modular unit for detaining people under civil immigration authority [S2].
It would cut off funding: no previously appropriated money could be spent or reprogrammed for new detention or holding facilities, whether run by ICE or a contractor [S2].
Money already obligated to operate new detention models would be transferred to needed services such as affordable health care and housing [S2].
Its findings cite medical neglect, overcrowding, deaths in detention (33 in 2025, 13 so far in 2026), and the lack of sewage and sanitation infrastructure in buildings not built for detention [S2].

analysis.who_pays: DHS and ICE would lose the authority and money to build the detention expansion they have announced, and the private contractors and construction firms that hold or seek those detention contracts would lose the business.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers not only detention centers but also new processing and holding facilities, so during enforcement operations with record detention populations, ICE would have no new capacity from any source — a cost an honest supporter acknowledges: existing facilities would absorb the strain [S2].

The bill's core prohibition applies only to 'new' detention models and facilities; it does not close or defund existing detention sites, so the conditions it condemns would continue in places already operating [S2].

Opponents of immigration enforcement restrictions argue that Congress conditioning and prohibiting the use of federal funds this way (the power the bill invokes) limits the executive's operational flexibility on border and removal policy [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill is the one its text makes: a roughly $38.3 billion program to house detainees in warehouses and tents, in facilities lacking basic sanitation, with deaths rising year over year, at direct expense to taxpayers and nearby communities. The strongest objection is practical: with detention populations elevated, cutting off all new capacity — including processing space — could force releases or worsen crowding in existing facilities, and the bill leaves existing detention untouched. The redirection of obligated funds to health care and housing is also an unusual use of an appropriations rider. On the bill's own terms it is a genuine restraint on a large spending program, but it is a narrow tool against a system-scale problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Homeland Security committees and then to a Judiciary subcommittee, where it sits with no scheduled markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on April 23, 2026, joined by 12 other House Democrats as original cosponsors [S2].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Homeland Security Committee [S4].
The next day, the House referred it to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability, where no further action is listed [S4].
The bill has 25 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support is shown on the record [S3].

The bill's findings state that ICE has announced plans to spend approximately $38.3 billion acquiring and retrofitting warehouses and industrial facilities into large-scale immigration detention centers [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no vote taken, the current arrangement stands: ICE keeps the authority and money to pursue its detention expansion, and the contractors in line for those contracts keep the opportunity. Because the Congress has not ended, the outcome is not final.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting new ICE detention models and recruited 12 fellow Democrats as original cosponsors

for.name: 25 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; all current cosponsors are Democrats

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: House majority, controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for any committee or floor action; the House majority decides which bills reach the floor, and none has

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability
against.role: Committee of referral where the bill sits
against.what_they_did: Received the referral the day after introduction; the record shows no markup or vote since

against.name: DHS and ICE
against.role: The agency the bill would restrict
against.what_they_did: Per the bill's findings, announced plans to spend approximately $38.3 billion acquiring and retrofitting warehouses and industrial facilities into large-scale detention centers, which the bill would prohibit

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors are House Democrats and there is no Republican support on the record; the bill was introduced by the House minority party, which does not control committee schedules or the floor calendar [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Private prison and immigration detention contractors
industries.note: These companies build and run detention sites under contract to ICE, and the bill would bar new contracts and renewals for warehouse, tent, and modular facilities and cut off funds for operating them. Their revenue in this line of business depends on expanding detention capacity, which is exactly what the bill stops. (The bill text names governmental and nongovernmental contractors as covered operators but does not name companies [S2].)

industries.industry: Construction and facility retrofit firms serving federal detention contracts
industries.note: The bill would end the acquisition and retrofitting of warehouses and industrial buildings into detention centers, a market the bill's findings peg at roughly $38.3 billion [S2].

industries.industry: Owners of warehouses and industrial property near detention sites
industries.note: Landlords who could lease or sell property to DHS for conversion would lose a buyer; local communities, per the bill's findings, would keep water, electricity, and tax revenue now at risk from detention operations [S2].

analysis.trajectory: A minority-party bill with only Democratic cosponsors, sitting in a Judiciary subcommittee with no scheduled markup, has very little path forward in a Congress where the House majority has taken no action. Bills at this stage almost always expire at the end of the Congress unless leadership decides otherwise; reintroduction in a future Congress is the usual next step if the position holds.
